entities.name: Arnulf of Chocques
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Arnulf of Chocques (died May 5, 1118), a pivotal ecclesiastical figure in the Latin East, served twice as the Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem (1099–1102 and 1112–1118) and initially as chaplain to Robert Curthose, Duke of Normandy. His career spanned the tumultuous immediate aftermath of the First Crusade, critically shaping the religious and political landscape of the nascent Kingdom of Jerusalem and establishing the hierarchical structure of the Latin Church in the Levant. He was central to the establishment of Western Christian authority in the Holy Land following its conquest, navigating complex power struggles between secular rulers and competing clerical factions.

Arnulf arrived in the Holy Land as chaplain to Duke Robert Curthose and quickly rose to prominence following the conquest of Jerusalem in July 1099. He played a key role in the immediate ecclesiastical organization, controversially overseeing the election of Godfrey of Bouillon as 'Advocate of the Holy Sepulchre' rather than King, a move that highlighted the nascent kingdom's unique spiritual claims. Arnulf was first elected Patriarch in August 1099, but his tenure was short-lived, marked by accusations of simony and an irregular election, leading to his deposition in favor of Daimbert of Pisa. Despite this setback, Arnulf's influence persisted; he served as a Papal Legate and was instrumental in the discovery and promotion of the Holy Lance, a relic of immense symbolic importance to the crusaders. He regained the Patriarchate in 1112, serving until his death, consolidating the Latin Church's presence and authority.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Arnulf of Chocques was instrumental in establishing the Latin Patriarchate of Jerusalem, a critical institution for the Crusader States, directly influencing the spiritual and political governance of the newly conquered territories. His leadership helped solidify Western Christian control in the Holy Land for nearly two centuries.
